title: Behavioural interviews (STAR) & your narrative
summary: Turn your maths-to-AI journey into clear STAR stories that prove you can deliver, learn fast, and work with a team.
objectives: Explain what behavioural interviews assess and why companies use them
Structure any answer with the STAR method (Situation, Task, Action, Result)
Build a personal narrative that links your maths degree, support role, and AI ambition
Prepare a story bank covering common competency themes
Quantify results and own the 'I' rather than 'we' in your answers
Answer the 'tell me about yourself' and 'why this role' questions confidently
Avoid the common traps: rambling, blaming others, and vague results

quiz.q: What does the STAR acronym stand for?
quiz.why: STAR = Situation, Task, Action, Result. It gives a clear beginning, middle, and end to a competency answer.

quiz.q: Which part of a STAR answer should usually take the most time?
quiz.why: Action is where you show what YOU specifically did — your skills and decisions. Keep Situation and Task brief context-setters.

quiz.q: In a STAR answer about a team project, should you say 'I' or 'we'?
quiz.why: Interviewers assess YOU. Credit the team for context, but use 'I' to describe the specific actions and decisions you owned.

quiz.q: Name one thing that makes a STAR 'Result' strong.
quiz.answer: A specific, quantified outcome (e.g. a number, percentage, time saved) and what you learned.
quiz.why: Vague results ('it went well') are forgettable. Numbers and a takeaway make the impact concrete and credible.

quiz.q: Why do interviewers ask behavioural questions instead of only technical ones?
quiz.answer: Past behaviour predicts future behaviour; they assess soft skills like communication, ownership, and how you handle setbacks.
quiz.why: Technical skill alone is not enough — teams need people who collaborate, learn, and stay calm under pressure.

quiz.q: What is the safest way to answer 'tell me about a weakness'?
options: Name a real weakness plus concrete steps you are taking to improve
Give a hidden strength like 'I work too hard'
quiz.why: Honesty plus a visible improvement plan shows self-awareness and growth — exactly what employers want to see.

body_markdown:
## Why behavioural interviews exist

Most AI and data roles include a **behavioural** (sometimes called *competency*) interview alongside the technical rounds. The core belief is simple: **past behaviour predicts future behaviour**. If you handled a tight deadline well before, you'll probably handle one well again.

These rounds test the things a coding test cannot: communication, ownership, teamwork, dealing with failure, and how you learn. For a maths graduate moving into AI from an L1 support role, this is great news — your support experience is full of exactly these stories.

## The STAR method

**STAR** gives every answer a clear shape so you don't ramble:

- **Situation** — set the scene in one or two sentences.
- **Task** — what was the goal or your responsibility?
- **Action** — what *you* did, step by step. This is the heart of it.
- **Result** — the outcome, ideally with a number, plus what you learned.

Keep Situation and Task short. Spend most of your words on **Action** and finish with a concrete **Result**.

## Build a story bank

Don't memorise scripts — prepare **raw material** you can adapt live. Aim for six to eight stories that, between them, cover the common themes: a success, a failure, a conflict, a deadline, learning something fast, and helping a customer or teammate.

Store them as structured notes so you can rehearse:

```python
story = {
    "theme": "learning fast",
    "situation": "L1 support; new ticketing tool with no docs",
    "task": "Cut my average resolution time within two weeks",
    "action": "Read the API logs, built a SQL cheat-sheet, paired with a senior",
    "result": "Resolution time dropped ~30%; I wrote the team's first runbook",
}
print(story["theme"], "->", story["result"])
```

## Quantify and own the 'I'

Vague results are forgettable. Wherever you can, attach a **number**: percentage faster, hours saved, tickets handled, accuracy gained. If you have no metric, use a clear before-and-after.

And watch your pronouns. Teams matter, but the interviewer is hiring **you**. Use *we* for context and *I* for the actions and decisions you personally owned.

## Your narrative thread

Your 'tell me about yourself' answer should be a **60-second story**, not your CV read aloud. Tie three things together: where you came from (maths), what you do now (support + self-taught AI), and where you're heading (this role).

```bash
# A simple structure to rehearse out loud
# Past:    "I have a maths degree and I love turning messy problems into clear models."
# Present: "In L1 support I learned to debug fast and explain things simply."
# Future:  "I have spent 30+ hours a week building AI projects and want to do it full time."
```

## Your task

Pick three of the common themes, write a STAR story for each, and **say them out loud and timed** — aim for 90 seconds each. Record yourself once; you'll hear the rambling instantly.

slides.title: Behavioural interviews & STAR
slides.narration: Welcome to Month Six, where we get you ready to apply and interview. This lesson is all about the behavioural interview, the round that tests how you work, not just what you know. By the end you'll be able to structure any answer with the STAR method and tell a clear story about your journey from maths graduate into A I.

slides.title: Why behavioural rounds?
bullets: Things a coding test cannot measure.
Your support role is full of stories.
slides.narration: So why do companies run these rounds at all? The core idea is that how you behaved in the past predicts how you'll behave in the future. They test the things a coding test simply can't: how you communicate, how you take ownership, how you handle a setback. For you, the L1 support experience is a goldmine of exactly these stories.

slides.title: The STAR method
bullets: Action: what YOU did — the core.
Result: outcome, ideally with a number.
slides.narration: The STAR method gives every answer a clean shape so you don't ramble. Situation sets the scene in a sentence or two. Task is the goal or your responsibility. Action is what you personally did, and this is the heart of the answer. Result is the outcome, ideally with a number, plus what you learned.

slides.title: Spend time on Action
slides.narration: Here's the mistake almost everyone makes: they spend two minutes on the Situation and ten seconds on what they actually did. Flip that. Keep the scene-setting brief, then spend the bulk of your answer on Action, the decisions and the skills you brought, and land it with a clear Result.

slides.title: Build a story bank
slides.narration: Don't memorise rigid scripts. Instead, prepare a bank of six to eight stories you can adapt live. Between them they should cover a success, a failure, a conflict, a tight deadline, and learning something fast. Store them as structured notes, like this little dictionary, so you can rehearse the key beats out loud and timed.

slides.title: Quantify your results
bullets: Attach a number wherever you can.
slides.narration: Vague results vanish from an interviewer's memory the moment you stop talking. Wherever you can, attach a number: a percentage faster, hours saved, tickets handled, accuracy gained. If you genuinely have no metric, paint a clear before and after. Concrete impact is what gets remembered and gets you hired.

slides.title: Own the 'I'
slides.narration: Watch your pronouns carefully. Teamwork matters, but the person across the table is hiring you, not your old team. Use we to set the context, then switch to I for the specific actions and decisions you personally owned. Hiding behind the team is the fastest way to sound like you did nothing.

slides.title: Your narrative thread
bullets: 'Tell me about yourself' is a 60-sec story.
slides.code:
# Past:    maths -> clear models
# Present: support -> debug & explain
# Future:  30+ hrs/wk on AI projects
slides.narration: Your tell me about yourself answer should be a sixty second story, not your C V read aloud. Tie three threads together. Past: the maths degree and your love of turning messy problems into clear models. Present: support, where you learned to debug fast and explain simply. Future: this exact role, and the thirty plus hours a week you've put into A I projects.

slides.title: Handling weaknesses
bullets: Name a real weakness, not a humblebrag.
slides.narration: When they ask about a weakness, resist the humblebrag like I work too hard. It fools nobody. Instead name a genuine weakness and, crucially, the concrete steps you're taking to improve it. Self-awareness plus a visible growth plan is far more impressive than pretending to be flawless.

slides.title: Common traps
slides.narration: Let's name the traps that sink good candidates. One: rambling with no structure, which STAR fixes. Two: blaming a manager or teammate, which makes you look like the problem. Three: vague results with no impact. And four: a memorised, robotic delivery. Prepare the material, but keep the delivery natural and conversational.
